opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core intuition is that consistency is a really useful signal even when you don't have ground truth. If you ask a model the same question several times, or have several models answer it independently, the places where they agree tend to be more reliable, and the places where they diverge are often exactly where something has gone wrong. A single answer gives a critic nothing to compare against. It just sees one confident-sounding chain of reasoning, and it's very hard to tell from the inside whether a step is a hallucination or a subtle arithmetic slip. But once you have several answers side by side, the disagreements localize the problem. The critic can say, "these three responses computed this intermediate value one way and this one did it differently, so let's look closely at that step."

This was part of the motivation behind our work on multi-agent debate. Rather than just sampling and taking a majority vote, you let the different instances read each other's responses and critique them over a few rounds. What we found is that models are actually much better at verifying or spotting flaws in someone else's reasoning than at generating a correct answer from scratch. So generation provides diversity, and the critique step exploits that diversity. Over rounds, answers tend to converge, and they converge more often toward the correct answer, with fewer hallucinated facts, than any single sample would give you.

I think of it a bit like an energy landscape. Each sample is a guess, and the critic is implicitly evaluating how compatible each guess is with the others and with the constraints of the problem. Correct answers tend to be mutually consistent because there's essentially one way to be right, while errors tend to be idiosyncratic, since there are many different ways to be wrong. That asymmetry is what lets you get a meaningful signal without knowing the answer in advance.

There are limits, of course. If the model has a systematic bias, all the samples might agree on the same wrong answer, and consistency won't save you. So you want genuine diversity, whether from different prompts, different models, or different reasoning strategies. But in practice, using multiple generations as a kind of self-generated reference set is one of the most effective ways to turn generation compute into better verification.

r001.rationale: The response says that disagreements among multiple answers can localize a problem and that divergence is a useful signal even without ground truth.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot. The basic problem is that when you ask a model a hard question, it gives you one answer, and if you don't know the ground truth, it's really hard to tell whether that answer is right. The model will state a wrong answer with exactly the same confidence as a right one. So verification in isolation is tough.

What generating multiple answers gives you is context. If I sample, say, five or ten responses to the same question and they all agree, that's at least weak evidence that the model has something stable it's computing toward. But the much more interesting case is when they disagree. Now the critic doesn't have to judge an answer in a vacuum. It can look at two solutions that reach different conclusions and ask, where exactly do these diverge? Which step in one of them doesn't follow from the previous step? That's a much more tractable problem than asking "is this correct" from scratch, because disagreement points you right at the part of the reasoning that's suspect.

There's also a nice asymmetry here that we lean on. Spotting an error is often easier than producing a correct solution. A critic that could never have solved the problem itself can still notice that two derivations contradict each other, or that one of them makes an arithmetic slip, or that one invokes a fact the other one rejects. So you're turning a generation problem into a comparison problem, and comparison is where language models tend to be more reliable.

And the last piece is that the errors across samples tend to be somewhat independent. A model might hallucinate a reference in one sample, but it's less likely to hallucinate the exact same reference in all of them. So the inconsistencies themselves become a signal. In our work on things like multi-agent debate, that's really the mechanism: you're not getting correctness from any single agent, you're getting it from the critic being able to triangulate across a population of attempts. That's a way of extracting more out of the model than any one forward pass gives you, without needing an external answer key.

r001.rationale: The response says disagreement between sampled answers lets the critic compare where they diverge and identify suspect reasoning, without needing an external answer key.

astra-6.text:
Well, even if you don’t know the correct answer, you can look at whether different answers agree with each other. If you generate several responses and they make conflicting claims, that gives the critic a signal that something needs closer examination. It can compare the reasoning, identify where the answers diverge, and look for inconsistencies that might be harder to notice in a single response.

Of course, agreement doesn’t guarantee correctness. The model could repeat the same mistake across all the answers. But generating multiple answers gives the critic more evidence to work with, even without access to a ground-truth answer.

r001.rationale: The response says conflicting claims across multiple generated answers signal that something needs closer examination, even without knowing the correct answer.

sol-6.1.text:
The intuition is that even if you don’t know the correct answer, you can look for inconsistencies across different answers. If you ask a model the same question several times, it might make different assumptions or take different reasoning paths. A critic can compare those and say, “These two claims can’t both be true,” or identify a step that one answer handles carefully and another skips.

So you’re giving the critic more evidence than it would have from inspecting a single response. That doesn’t mean agreement guarantees correctness—the model could repeat the same mistake every time. But differences between answers can help expose where the reasoning is fragile and where further checking is needed.

r001.rationale: The response says a critic can compare multiple answers and identify claims that cannot both be true, exposing a problem without knowing the correct answer.
